headline: Return the plaintext the recipient's own key unwraps, sign the content a caller passed rather than one substituted after it, verify an alternative signature another implementation made, and refuse the key-possession requests the linter let through.
summary: Correctness fixes across the CMS, timestamp, transparency-log, Sigstore, TUF, JOSE, ACME, HPKE, CRMF, certificate-path and ASN.1 surfaces. `pki.cms.decrypt` could return the wrong plaintext to a recipient whose key unwrap had already failed, about one time in 256 for a non-AEAD content. Seven verbs that take content and a description of what to do with it held the content as a view of the caller's buffer and read the description afterwards, so a field supplied through an accessor replaced what they went on to sign, encrypt, authenticate or compress. `pki.asn1.decodeOidContent` took its length from a property a caller can set independently of the bytes, so it could return an OID the buffer does not encode, and an OID selects an algorithm. The alternative signature on a certificate or CRL now covers the `PreTBSCertificate` and `PreTBSCertList` that `draft-truskovsky-lamps-pq-hybrid-x509` defines, so one made by this toolkit verifies in Bouncy Castle and one made there verifies here. `pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` assembled a certification path by taking the first intermediate matching an issuer name, so a bundle carrying two intermediates with one subject, which is what a rotated CA looks like, was refused for want of a chain it carried. And the RFC 9883 key-possession surface read one attribute of several and one field where the requirement turns on two, so `pki.possession.verifyRequest` accepted requests it should refuse, `pki.lint.csr` graded conforming what that verb rejects, and `pki.csr.sign` emitted them under a profile that advertises the requirement.

Fixed: `pki.tuf.checkExpiry` read the `expires` beside the signed body rather than the one inside it, so the freeze-attack check and the signature check could be about different documents. A parsed object carries both, and only the body's is covered by the signature: metadata correctly signed with an expiry in 2020, with that copy moved to 2099, was reported `verified` and passed the expiry check at a 2026 instant, which is the defense answering about a date the document does not carry. The expiry now comes from `metadata.signed`, and a copy the object also states must agree with it, as must a stated `specVersion`; either contradicting the body is `tuf/bad-input`. `metadata.signed` is required as a result, and no field of the metadata object either verb reads may be an accessor: reading one is caller code running mid-verb, and with several fields read in sequence a getter on one could change the body while another was being read, so the verb answered about a document the object carried neither before nor after. A document `pki.tuf.parseMetadata` returned carries plain values, so a conforming caller sees no change; an object supplying one through a getter is `tuf/bad-input`. Every convenience copy the object carries beside the body is checked against it, not only `specVersion`: `type`, `version` and `expires` too, since a caller reads `version` for a rollback comparison and `type` to choose which role a document belongs to, and a copy contradicting the body describes a document the caller does not hold. A `signedBytes` the object carries is held to the body as well, so the two verbs agree about which objects they will answer for: the expiry check read the body while the bytes beside it encoded another document, and reported on it. The object must be a plain record for the same reason: a Proxy answers from a trap rather than from a property, so one handing over a supported body when asked while carrying an unsupported one otherwise had both verbs answer about a document it never held. Each signature record is held to the same rule, its fields being read inside the loop that verifies, and a record that is not a plain object with plain fields is `tuf/bad-metadata`.

`pki.tuf.updateRoot` adopted a root that states a role only for itself. The TUF specification section 4.3 requires one for each of `root`, `snapshot`, `targets` and `timestamp`, calling the `mirrors` role optional, and a root missing any of the four leaves a client holding a trust anchor that cannot authenticate the rest of the repository's metadata: there is no key list and no threshold to check a targets, snapshot or timestamp document against. All four are required now, each stating a `keyids` array and a `threshold` that is a positive integer, since a role record naming neither is present without being usable. A root missing one, or carrying an unusable record for one, is `tuf/bad-metadata`. A record is unusable when its `keyids` list is empty, holds anything that is not a key identifier string, or names an identifier the root's own `keys` map does not carry, and when its threshold asks for more signatures than the list names distinct keys: a verdict counts each identifier once, so a role naming one key twice for a threshold of two can never be met. The specification states the first two of those, calling a key identifier the hexdigest of a hash and a threshold a positive integer of at least one; the rest is this build refusing a record it could never use, and the refusals say which is which. Each identifier is recomputed from the key filed under it, because carrying the identifier is not the same as being that key: only the root role is verified during a rotation, so a targets, snapshot or timestamp role naming a key filed under an identifier that is not its own was adopted and failed later, where the client had already trusted the root. That is `tuf/bad-key`, the code the same condition already draws where a role is verified. Each key is also held to the checks the verify makes before it looks at a signature: the keytype and scheme are ones this build reads, the material imports, the declared type matches what imported, and an ed25519 point is on the curve. An identifier is a hash of a key's canonical form and says nothing about any of that, so a role could name a key filed under its own identifier that verifies nothing.

`pki.tuf.verifySignatures` counted key identifiers toward a role's threshold, and an identifier is a hash of the whole key object, so one public key can hold two of them: adding a member the hash covers and the cryptography ignores, such as a comment, yields a second identifier for the same key. A role naming both with a threshold of two was then met by one key, the same signature bytes verifying under each entry, which is a threshold of two satisfied by one signer. A comment is one of five spellings: a PEM with CRLF line endings, a space before each newline, an EC point written compressed rather than uncompressed, and the `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256` keytype where another entry says `ecdsa` each give the same point a different identifier. The count is over the key's own coordinates now, taken from the imported key, so every spelling of one key collapses to one, and `pki.tuf.updateRoot` compares a role's threshold against the same count when it adopts a root. An exported SubjectPublicKeyInfo would not do: the runtime preserves a compressed point through an export, 59 bytes against 91, while the coordinates of the two are identical. The identifiers that counted are still what the verdict reports, two genuinely different keys still meet a threshold of two, and a key carrying nothing but its material is unaffected.

`pki.hpke`'s hybrid KEMs combined their two shared secrets through a concatenation that reached `Buffer.concat` as a live property, and the combiner's digest likewise reached the hash prototype's own `update`. A replacement of either decides what the combiner covers: one answering the combiner's five-part input with a constant makes encapsulation and decapsulation derive the same publicly known value instead of binding `ssPQ` to `ssT`, so every HPKE key that follows is predictable and the ciphertext's confidentiality is gone. Both go through operations captured at load now, and the module's single concatenation helper carries that for all nine of its call sites, the key schedule and the KEM suite identifier among them.

`pki.cms.encrypt` and `pki.cms.authenticate` assembled the argument list they fix with `Array.prototype.concat`, so a replacement of that method chose the list: one that kept the caller's recipients and options while putting other bytes in the content slot made `encrypt` encrypt those bytes and `authenticate` compute a valid MAC over them. The content is what both verbs exist to protect, and the list is written out as a literal now, which is not a dispatch and has nothing to replace. The same assembly decided three more values and each goes through the captured operation: the sub-identifier list `pki.asn1` encodes an OID from, which names the algorithm a signature is made under; the candidate chain the certification-path search carries in `pki.path.validate`; and the signed attribute set in `pki.tsp.sign`, whose first entry is the signing-certificate attribute binding the token to the certificate it names. `pki.cms.authenticate` computed the `messageDigest` attribute through the hash prototype's own `update` and `digest`, which are writable too, so a replacement chose what that digest covered and the message then carried a digest of other bytes under a valid MAC: `pki.cms.decrypt` refuses such a message, so what it cost was a document that does not verify against the content it holds. The digest is taken through operations captured at load, which is `guard.crypto.digest`.

`pki.tlog.verifyNote` read the caller's key records before it copied the note, so a record supplying its `name` or `publicKey` through an accessor ran while the caller's buffer was still the caller's and could replace the note under verification: the verdict then reported on a document that was not the argument. Measured, a getter that copied a validly signed note over an invalidly signed one turned `tlog/bad-signature` into `verified`. The note is copied first, before any key record is read, which is the order `pki.tlog.verifyCheckpoint` already used. Reading each key once bounds what a key can state about itself and says nothing about what reading it can do to the note.

`pki.relatedCert.verifyRequest` accepted a correctly signed proof however old its `requestTime` was, so a captured `relatedCertRequest` attribute copied into a new certification request for another key verified indefinitely. The proof covers the `certID` and the `requestTime` and nothing else, which is what makes the time the whole replay defense. RFC 9763 section 3.2 makes the check the certification authority's, "MUST check that the BinaryTime indicated in the requestTime field is sufficiently fresh", and the same clause leaves the window to local policy, so the verb now requires `opts.maxAge` in seconds rather than choosing a window: a call without one is refused with `relatedcert/no-freshness-policy`, because a verifier that cannot make a required check must not report success. `opts.at` names the instant judged against, for reading a request recorded earlier. A `requestTime` outside the window, or ahead of the instant, is `relatedcert/stale-request`. The time is read once, into the value both the check and the verified bytes use.

`pki.tuf.parseMetadata` read a document whose `spec_version` names a specification version this build does not implement, or which names none at all, under this build's rules, and `pki.tuf.updateRoot` adopted such a root. The TUF specification section 4.3 has clients verify that the field matches the version they implement and leaves the definition of a match to the adopter; this build implements 1.x, so the major version is the match and a later 1.x minor is still read, while another major version is refused with `tuf/unsupported-spec-version`. The same clause states the field's format, "Its format follows the Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 (semver) specification", so the whole string is held to that grammar and a value that is not a version is malformed rather than unsupported: `1.`, `1.0`, `1.foo`, `1.0.0oops`, `1.0.0.0` and a value with a trailing space are each refused, while a pre-release or build part is read, `1.0.0-rc.1` and `1.2.3+0010` included. A document omitting the field is refused as malformed too, the field being mandatory. The clause covers metadata rather than root metadata, so the match is made at the parse, which every role comes through: `pki.tuf.verifySignatures` and `pki.tuf.checkExpiry` can no longer be handed a targets, snapshot or timestamp document written to another major version, where a key identifier is a hash of this version's canonical form and an expiry is read in the format this version states. It is made before `_type`, `version` and `expires` are read, each of those being a rule of this version too. `metadata.specVersion` carries the matched string, so it is never null. `pki.tuf.verifySignatures` and `pki.tuf.checkExpiry` take a metadata object rather than bytes, and both are reachable with one a caller assembled rather than one `pki.tuf.parseMetadata` produced, so both make the match too: without it, a document carrying a real signature and declaring `2.0.0` was reported `verified`, and its expiry check returned `true`. An object with no version at all is `tuf/bad-input` there, the caller's object being incomplete rather than a document malformed.

`pki.tuf.verifySignatures` read the bytes it verifies and the version it reads them under from two places. A parsed document is the caller's object once it is returned, and `signedBytes` is a Buffer whose contents can be overwritten, so `specVersion` named the document that was parsed while `signedBytes` named the document that got verified. Measured: a root declaring `1.0.31` whose bytes were replaced with a validly signed `2.0.31` document was reported `verified` with the field still reading `1.0.31`, which is the attack `pki.tuf` already refuses for the `version` field. The document verified is now derived from one read of `metadata.signed`, and `metadata.signedBytes` must equal that canonical form, so the bytes the signatures are checked over are the ones the object states and the version is read from the same copy. A mismatch is `tuf/bad-input`. `metadata.signed` is required as a result, and a `metadata.specVersion` that contradicts the body it carries is refused rather than preferred.
Metadata that omitted the field parsed before this release and is refused now; a TUF repository publishes it on every document.

`pki fetch --der` wrote several concatenated DER certificates when the chain had more than one, which is not a DER document: `pki parse` and `pki convert` reject the file with `x509/bad-der`, so the output could not be read back by the tool that produced it. A chain of more than one certificate is refused under `--der` now, naming the PEM form, and a single certificate is written as it always was.

`pki.ct.getRoots` decoded however many certificates a log's accepted-roots response named. The element count was bounded only where an entry has a fixed width, which the proof verbs' entries do and the roots response's do not, so keying the bound on that width left this one caller outside it. A configured log is trusted for its signatures rather than for its resource use, and a response body well inside the transport's size cap carries about a million empty strings, each of which became its own buffer. The count is now bounded by `C.LIMITS.CT_MAX_ROOTS`, far above the few hundred roots a public log lists, and an oversized response is refused with `ct/bad-roots` before any entry is decoded. The proof verbs keep the bound they had.

`pki.cms.decrypt` and `pki.smime.decrypt` refuse a message that uses RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 key transport over a content with no integrity tag, such as AES-CBC, unless the caller passes `allowUnauthenticatedRsa15`. That combination offers no way to be both correct and safe: the content padding is its only integrity check, so either a recipient whose key unwrap failed can pass it and the verb returns the plaintext of a substituted key, or it cannot and acceptance then tells an attacker submitting chosen ciphertexts that theirs decoded, which is the Bleichenbacher distinction RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 is vulnerable to (RFC 8017 sec. 7.2). Measured against an `openssl cms -encrypt -aes-256-cbc` message, 256 chosen ciphertexts per arm: one acceptance where the unwrap conformed against none where it did not. The refusal is made before the unwrap, so under the default nothing in the verdict depends on the unwrap at all, measured at zero acceptances on both arms. `openssl cms -encrypt` and `openssl smime -encrypt` emit exactly this combination when no algorithm is named, so reading one of their messages needs the option; the toolkit's own `pki.cms.encrypt` uses RSAES-OAEP with AES-GCM and is unaffected, and an AEAD content or an OAEP recipient needs no option because each carries its own integrity check. Re-encrypting to `aes-256-gcm` removes the question.

`pki.tlog.verifyNote` and `pki.tlog.verifyCheckpoint` could accept a note carrying a signature that was never checked. A note separates its text from its signature lines with a blank line and ends with a newline, so splitting the signature half leaves one empty element after the last line, and the parser dropped it by calling `Array.prototype.pop`. That is an ordinary writable property of the array prototype: a replacement that pops twice takes the final signature line away with the empty element, so a note whose last line is a forged signature under a key the caller supplied verified instead of drawing `tlog/bad-signature`. The drop now goes through a captured operation, as the rest of the module's reads already did, and every signature line reaches the check whatever the prototype holds. The same applies to every other place in the toolkit that moved or reordered an element of a list through a live prototype method: the certification-path search stacks in `pki.path.validate`, the nonce pool in the `pki.acme` client, the DER length and OID encoders in `pki.asn1`, the signer-set search in `pki.tsp`, the trust-path ordering in `pki.webauthn` and its metadata chain walk, and the tile-path reader in `pki.tlog`.

`pki.tuf.parseMetadata` and `pki.tuf.checkExpiry` read the metadata `expires` field with the runtime's own date parser, which accepts far more than the format the TUF specification states and, for an impossible date, rolls it forward rather than refusing it. Metadata expiring on `2026-02-30` was therefore read as expiring on March 2 and treated as usable for two days it does not state, and a date with no time or a time with no zone was accepted, where the instant then depends on the reader's timezone rather than on the document. The specification section 4.2.3 fixes the format as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ` in UTC, and the field is now held to it through the same RFC 3339 reader the rest of the toolkit uses, calendar validity and leap years included: February 29 is accepted in a leap year and refused outside one. A zero numeric offset is accepted alongside `Z`, both denoting the same instant.

A value that holds the same subobject in more than one place could exhaust the process. Both the deep copy every verb takes of a caller's object and `pki.tuf.canonicalJson` walk each reference independently, so such a value is a graph rather than a tree and expands once per reference, while the only bound either had was on nesting DEPTH. Measured, an array built by nesting the same array in itself twenty-five times, twenty-five arrays in all, made `pki.tuf.canonicalJson` end the process with a fatal out-of-memory on a 2 GiB heap, and `pki.jose.thumbprint` and `pki.tuf.keyId` spend six seconds and doubling on the same value placed in a member beside the ones they read. Both walks now charge a shared budget and refuse before accumulating: the canonical form is bounded by the same 1 MiB a TUF document is read under, and a copy by the number of values it visits, `C.LIMITS.DEEP_COPY_MAX_NODES`. The worst case is a constant rather than a function of the input, measured at about 400 milliseconds for a copy and milliseconds for the canonical form, and the inputs an operator has are well inside both: a thousand-record trust-anchor list copies in 54 milliseconds. The refusals are `tuf/too-large` and each verb's own bad-input code.

`pki.relatedCert.verifyRequest` refused a conforming request whose issuer name is encoded differently from the certificate's. It compared the `IssuerAndSerialNumber` the request carries against the certificate's by their DER bytes, so a certificate holding its issuer common name as a `PrintableString` and a request naming the same common name as a `UTF8String` were read as different certificates and the proof was rejected with `relatedcert/cert-mismatch`. RFC 9763 sec. 3.2 has the certification authority compare the value rather than the encoding, and the field is a `Name`, so RFC 5280 sec. 7.1 governs: the serial numbers are compared as integers and the issuer under the same distinguished-name rules the rest of the toolkit uses. A different issuer name is still refused. The bytes the proof signature covers are unchanged, being the request's own as sec. 3.1 states, so only the identity comparison folds encodings.

`pki.altSig.subjectAltPublicKey` returned an issuer alternative key read out of a CRL. The `subjectAltPublicKeyInfo` extension is certificate-only, and the verb documents that a CRL is refused, but the refusal came from the extension being absent rather than from the structure being the wrong kind: a CRL carrying one, which the pre-encoded extensions array admits under `profile: "none"`, had it decoded with the certificate decoder and its key handed back. A key is an identity, so which structure it was read from decides what it means. The kind is checked before any extension is read now, and which kinds may carry the extension is a field on the structure's own registry row rather than a position in a list.

`pki.merkle.root`, `pki.merkle.inclusionProof` and `pki.merkle.consistencyProof` held each leaf as a view of the caller's own buffer rather than a copy, and folded them in a later pass. Leaves supplied through accessors that hand out one reused buffer therefore all pointed at the same bytes by the time the fold ran, so collecting the second leaf overwrote the first: measured, the root of two distinct leaves came out as the root of the second leaf twice, with nothing reporting it. Each leaf, proof node and supplied hash is copied as it is read now, so every byte these verbs fold, hash or compare is their own. A leaf is 32 bytes, so the copy costs nothing measurable.

`pki.merkle` assembled its proofs through the live array prototype, so a replacement installed after the module loaded chose which nodes a proof carried and in what order: one returning its receiver made `pki.merkle.inclusionProof` return an empty proof for a two-leaf tree. The module now takes every operation it decides with at load, as the rest of the toolkit does, which also brings it inside the gate that keeps it that way.

`pki.merkle.root`, `pki.merkle.inclusionProof` and `pki.merkle.consistencyProof` could commit to a tree the caller never supplied. Each checked the leaf array's length against the leaf cap and then walked it with a loop that read the length again on every iteration, so a leaf supplied through an accessor that shortens the array left the cap approving four leaves and the walk collecting one: the root returned was the first leaf's, and both proof producers folded the same short tree. The count is now read once, before any leaf is touched, through the same helper that already read each leaf once, and an array that shrinks under the walk is refused rather than folded short. Reading it twice did not need a leaf accessor at all: `Array.isArray` is true for a `Proxy` whose target is an array, and such a proxy answers `length` afresh on each read, so measured, a cap that saw zero leaves passed while the fold built a one-leaf tree. Whichever count a caller's object reports is now the one the cap judges and the one the fold uses. The verifiers took a proof array through the same shape and were never exposed by it, a proof collected short folding to a root that does not match the one supplied, and they go through the helper too.

`pki.x509.sign` ignored an `issuer.altPublicKey` supplied without an `issuer.altKey` beside it, emitting an ordinary certificate with no alternative signature and reporting success. An alternative signature needs both halves, the private key to sign with and the public half to resolve the algorithm from, and a configuration assembled a field at a time is where one of them goes missing. The pair is now refused with `x509/bad-input` naming the missing field, which is what `pki.crl.sign` already did for the same pair. The reverse pairing, an `altKey` with no `altPublicKey`, was already refused and is unchanged.

`pki.cms.decrypt` could return the wrong plaintext for a recipient whose key unwrap had already failed. On an RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 fault the toolkit substitutes a fresh random content-encryption key and proceeds, so that the failure costs the same work and the same time as a success and no recipient, padding or structure oracle is left. The content decrypt then decided whether that candidate was the right one, and a random key leaves a final CBC block that is valid PKCS#7 padding about one time in 256, so a known-bad recipient won that often: measured 2 of 400 streamed decrypts of a two-recipient AES-256-CBC message returned the wrong plaintext and named the rejected recipient as the one used. A candidate the substitute stood in for is now never the answer, measured 400 of 400 correct on both the buffered and the streamed path. The substitute keeps doing its job: the decrypt still runs, and on the streamed path the chunks are still delivered and the failure still arrives on consumption, so the error code, the stage and the number of bytes delivered are the same as for any other wrong key, measured identical over 700 draws. Padding is the only check a non-AEAD content offers, which is why AES-GCM is the encrypt default: it rejects a wrong content key on the tag.

Seven verbs that take content and a description of what to do with it held the content as a view of the caller's own buffer, and read the description afterwards. Reading it is caller code when a field is supplied through an accessor, so it runs between the content being accepted and being used, and over a view it replaced what the verb went on to sign, encrypt, authenticate or compress. `pki.cms.encrypt` encrypted substituted plaintext under both the CBC and the AEAD content algorithms; `pki.cms.authenticate` digested, MACed and embedded substituted content; `pki.smime.sign`, `pki.smime.encrypt` and `pki.smime.compress` did the same, including under `protectHeaders`; `pki.jose.sign` signed a substituted payload; and `pki.tls.compressCertificate` compressed a substituted certificate message. No timing is involved, the accessor running at a fixed point in each verb, and it matters for a caller that holds content it trusts beside a descriptor or an option object it does not. Every one of them now takes the content before any caller description is read, so they act on the content they were handed whichever object the accessor sits on, and `pki.cms.encrypt` and `pki.cms.authenticate` refuse an options object that supplies a field through an accessor with `cms/bad-input` rather than reading it. `pki.cms.sign` was never affected, having copied its content at entry since it shipped, and `pki.cms.decrypt` fails closed on the same route with `cms/decrypt-failed`. A content passed as a stream is a different case and is not covered: its bytes do not exist until the iterator is pulled, which is after the recipients have been read, so a caller that mutates a buffer it is about to yield yields the mutated bytes and there is nothing earlier for the verb to take. Pass such a content as a Buffer where the recipient descriptor is not trusted. Each chunk is handled as it arrives, so a buffer reused across yields carries the value it held at each one.

`pki.jose.verify` read a supplied JWK's `crv` eight times and its `kty` nine times on one successful verification, and the first of those reads is what selects which curve the Edwards low-order point check validates the key against. A caller object answering that read differently from the later ones therefore had its key checked under one curve's parameters and imported under another: a JWK whose `crv` answered `Ed448` once and `Ed25519` afterwards verified, with the point check bypassed. That check is what stops a low-order key from verifying a forged signature. The key is now copied once, before any member of it is read, so the check, the import and the algorithm selection all read one key; a key whose members are accessors is refused as `jose/bad-key`.

An HPKE context dropped its additional authenticated data instead of binding it, when that data was held in a `DataView` or an `ArrayBuffer`. `context.seal` and `context.open` decided whether to bind the AAD by testing `aad.length`, which is `undefined` for both containers, so the AEAD was set up with no additional data and the tag authenticated none. Both sides dropped it alike, so the message still opened and a caller exercising their own code saw the round trip succeed while the binding they relied on was absent: a ciphertext could then be opened under any other AAD. The AAD is now normalized before its width decides anything, so it binds whichever container holds it, and a message sealed under one AAD no longer opens under another. An absent or empty AAD still means no additional data, as RFC 9180 sec. 5.2 specifies. `pki.cms` and `pki.webcrypto` were unaffected: the CMS additional data is the DER this toolkit builds, and the WebCrypto surface already normalized it.

`pki.tuf.canonicalJson` encoded any object by its own enumerable keys, so a `Date`, a `Map` and a `Set` each became `{}` and a Buffer became a map of its byte indices. Canonical JSON is the preimage a TUF signature covers, so a field encoding to `{}` is a field the signature does not cover while it remains in the caller's document: the signed form and the document the caller believes they signed differed, with nothing reporting it. The encoder already refused a float, a function, `undefined`, a BigInt, `NaN` and `Infinity`; a built-in object is now refused the same way. Plain objects, including null-prototype records, and arrays are unaffected.

`pki.asn1.decodeOidContent` read its byte count from the input's `length` property. A Buffer accepts an own `length` that differs from its real size, and every other read of a buffer's bytes, indexing, `subarray`, `concat` and `toString`, uses the real count; only `length` can disagree. So a buffer whose bytes encode `1.2.840.3` and whose `length` reported 3 decoded as `1.2.840`, handing back an OID the bytes do not encode while an OID selects a signature algorithm and an extension decoder. The count is now taken once from the authoritative source, so the bytes decide.

`pki.tsp.verify` checked only the `signingCertificateV2` attribute of a token that carries both binding attributes, so a token naming the real signer in its v2 attribute and a different certificate in its v1 attribute verified. Both sit among the signed attributes, so the timestamping authority signed the contradiction, and a verifier reading only the legacy attribute resolves a certificate this one never checked. A token whose two binding attributes name different certificates is refused with `tsp/cert-binding-mismatch` now, rather than resolved in favor of one of them, whichever order the signed attributes are sorted in and by every claim an attribute makes: an `ESSCertID` states the signer as a certificate hash and again as an issuer and serial, and both are compared against the certificate that signed the token. A token carrying both attributes and naming the same certificate in each still verifies, and the verdict still rests on the v2 attribute and its own digest.

`pki.tsp.verify` accepted a SHA-1 `messageImprint`, and `allowWeakDigests` did not gate it. The imprint is the only thing binding a timestamp token to the data it timestamps, so a collision in that digest substitutes the data under a genuine token, and the option reached only the token's own signature digest: a SHA-1 imprint verified under the default, under `allowWeakDigests: false` and under `true` alike. It is now refused by default and verified under `allowWeakDigests`, which is the same opt-in an archived signature already needs, and it does not make a mismatched imprint verify. No fetched clause forbids SHA-1 here, the one quoted algorithm prohibition being ETSI EN 319 122-1 clause 6.2.1 on MD5, so this is stated as the toolkit's posture rather than as a requirement.

`pki.jose.sign` read `opts.key` four times: once to test that it is a key, twice for the check that binds the key's hash to the header's `alg`, and once more to sign with. A caller object answering those reads differently had the binding checked against a key that did not sign, and the signed message then declared an algorithm its signature was not made under. The RSA algorithms were where it showed, since the registry's fixed signature widths catch the HMAC and elliptic-curve cases and two 2048-bit RSA keys produce the same signature length. A conforming verifier rejects such a message, including `pki.jose.verify`, so it is not a signature another party accepts; what was wrong is that the key the check approved was never the key that signed. The option is read once now, before anything inspects it, and the hash check, the signing and the width check all read that one key. A key whose `algorithm.hash` disappeared between two of those reads previously produced an untyped `TypeError` from a public verb rather than a `jose/*` fault.

`pki.jose.thumbprint` checked each JWK member and then read it again to build the hash, so the RFC 7638 identifier could be computed over values the checks never approved. The thumbprint is how `pki.jose.verify` decides that an embedded key and a supplied key are the same key, and how an ACME key authorization names an account, so an identifier over unchecked values names a key that was never validated. The key is copied once at the door. The published RFC 7638 and RFC 8037 known answers are unchanged.

`pki.possession.verifyRequest` compared the subject alternative names a request asks for against the signature certificate's by rendering each entry to a string, so one comparison rule stood in for every GeneralName form. A dNSName differing only in case reported `subjectAltNamesMatch: false`, and so `valid: false`, although RFC 4343 makes DNS comparison case-insensitive; an rfc822Name differing only in the case of its host and a URI differing only in the case of its scheme or host did the same; and a directoryName re-encoded to equivalent bytes read as a second name although RFC 5280 sec. 7.1 compares one attribute at a time. Each form is now compared under its own rule, so the pairs that differ only where their rule folds match, and the pairs that differ where their rule is exact, an rfc822Name local part and a URI path among them, still do not. A form with no comparison rule of its own is compared by its encoded bytes, and a value a rule cannot be applied to is reported as unmatched rather than resolved either way.

`pki.lint.csr` under the `rfc9883` profile graded conforming two requests that `pki.possession.verifyRequest` refuses, so `pki.csr.sign(..., { profile: "rfc9883" })` emitted both although the profile advertises the requirement. A request whose subject key can only ever sign, naming no keyUsage at all, met neither the sec. 4 requirement that "the subjectPKInfo MUST contain the public key for the key establishment algorithm" nor the sec. 6 prohibition on obtaining a signature certificate, and was reported as having no findings; the row read only the key usages a request asks for. A request carrying more than one `statementOfPossession` attribute was likewise unreported, and which of several a CA should honor is stated nowhere, so every check the section asks for would have been made against one statement while the CA certified a request carrying another. Both are now errors, `lint/rfc9883/signature-certificate-requested` and the new `lint/rfc9883/statement-attribute-repeated`, and the linter and the verifier read one table of the signature-only key algorithms.

`pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` reported an unattested log index for a Rekor v2 entry. A v1 entry's signed entry timestamp covers the entry's own `logIndex`, so that value is attested; a v2 entry carries no such signature, and the verdict read the entry's number anyway, so a bundle could write any value there and have it returned as the index of the entry that verified. The verdict now carries an attested index on both paths: the entry's own where the signed entry timestamp covers it, and the leaf index the inclusion proof folded against the checkpoint-attested root where it does not. The two are different quantities, the log's counter and a leaf position, so neither is compared against the other.

The numbers `pki.ct`, `pki.sigstore` and `pki.webauthn` read as integers are now held to denoting exactly the integer they are read as. A token written `1.0000000000000001` becomes the number 1, so an integer check made after parsing sees a conforming document, and for a signed tree head that value is folded back into the bytes the signature covers: the rounded spelling verified while the value reported was not the one the log sent. The same applies to a Sigstore log index and integrated time, which enter the canonical form a signed entry timestamp covers, and to a FIDO metadata `no`, which is the rollback counter a relying party compares against the catalogue it already holds. An integer too large to represent exactly is refused for the same reason, since `9007199254740993` reads back as `9007199254740992`.

These are ordinary JSON formats where exponent form is legal, and nothing a conforming producer may emit is refused: `1e3`, `1.0` and `1500e-2` are read as their integers, and fields that are genuinely fractional are untouched. The rule names the members it applies to rather than the document, because these formats carry fractional values elsewhere by design: a FIDO metadata statement states biometric false-reject and false-accept rates as fractions, and an in-toto predicate inside a Sigstore bundle is arbitrary JSON.

A `tree_size` of `1.5` is now `ct/bad-json` rather than `ct/bad-sth`: a token that does not denote an integer is a malformed document, while one that denotes an integer the field cannot take, such as `-1`, is still a bad tree head.

`pki.altSig.signedData` built the bytes an alternative signature covers as the whole structure with its outer signature BIT STRING removed, keeping the `signature` AlgorithmIdentifier that the `tbsCertificate` carries. ITU-T X.509 (2019) clause 7.2.2 says to exclude "the signature component" without saying which of the two members of that name it is, and `draft-truskovsky-lamps-pq-hybrid-x509` gives the excluded one a type: the `PreTBSCertificate` of section 4 is the `tbsCertificate` without its `signature` field, the third element, and the `PreTBSCertList` of section 5 is the `tbsCertList` without its second. Both creation procedures add that field after the alternative signature is computed, so at that point there is none to cover. `pki.altSig.signedData` and `pki.altSig.verify` now build those bytes and `pki.x509.sign` and `pki.crl.sign` sign them, so an alternative signature on a certificate or CRL from this toolkit verifies in Bouncy Castle, and one Bouncy Castle made verifies here. A signature over the previous bytes is refused rather than accepted under a second scope.

`pki.tlog.verifyCheckpoint` read `opts.origin` four times, to see whether it was supplied, for its type, for its length, and for the comparison against the checkpoint. An accessor answers each read separately, so a caller object could present one origin to all three checks and the checkpoint's own origin to the comparison: the pinned origin was never the origin enforced, and the verdict reported a checkpoint as matching a log it does not name. The option is read once and the checks and the comparison both read that.

`pki.tuf.verifySignatures` read `opts.role` four times, for the presence check, the type check, and then each of `keyids` and `threshold`. `role` carries the authorization, so an accessor could present a strict role to the checks and a lax one to the field reads, combining one role's authorized keys with another's threshold: a document carrying one signature was reported `verified` against a role that required two. The role is captured once and every field is read off that capture.

`pki.tuf.checkExpiry` read `metadata.expires` three times: once to check it is a date string, once for the comparison, and once for the refusal message. A caller object could pass the type check with one date and hand the comparison a later one, and the verb then returned `true` for metadata that had expired. Expiry is the freeze-attack check, so a true verdict there answered about a date the document does not carry. The field is read once.

`pki.tuf.keyId` validated a key's `keytype`, `scheme` and `keyval` and then hashed the key, reading every field a second time. The identifier it returns is what a role's `keyids` list authorizes, so a key could validate as one shape and be hashed as another, naming a key that never passed validation. The key is copied before it is validated, and a key whose members are accessors is refused as `tuf/bad-key`.

`pki.acme.validate` read each field three times, for the closed status enum, the refusal message and the type check, while a conditionally-required field's predicate read the object again. A caller object could therefore pass the status enum as `valid`, answer the predicate so that a required field became optional, and present a third value to the type check, and the object was reported as conforming. Every field is now read once, before any check runs, and all of the checks decide from that reading. `pki.acme.validateProblem`, `pki.acme.identify` and `pki.acme.validateRenewalInfo` each read a member twice and now read it once; a non-string reaching the second read previously produced an untyped `TypeError` rather than an `acme/*` fault. The object is still returned as supplied.

The `pki.acme` request builders validated an option and then serialized it into the payload they sign, reading it twice, so a caller object could satisfy the validator with one value and have the signed request carry another. `revokeCert` is the sharpest case: the RFC 5280 CRLReason check exists to exclude the single unassigned value 7, and that is the value which could reach the certification authority. The same gap put unvalidated contacts, identifiers and dates into signed `newAccount`, `newOrder`, `newAuthz`, `updateAccount`, `challengeResponse`, `deactivate` and `postAsGet` payloads, so the mailto hygiene, the RFC 3339 checks and the boolean gates these verbs document were each enforced against a value that was never sent. Every one of them now passes its options through the gate the client methods already used, which refuses an options object whose fields are accessors rather than reading them once. The client methods were never affected.

`pki.acme` client `renewalWindow` validated `opts.previous` before fetching renewal information and read it three more times afterwards, so the prior window its stickiness decision compares against need not have been the one validated, and a value that stopped being an object across the fetch produced an untyped `TypeError`. The option is read once, before the fetch.

`pki.tlog.inclusionProof` read its `read` callback twice, once to check that it is a function and once to fetch tiles with, so the function checked need not have been the function called. The callback is read once.

`pki.crmf.verifyPop` read the first `statementOfPossession` control of a request that carries several and returned, so every later statement went unchecked: a request whose first statement is sound and whose second names a different certificate reported `verified: true` on the strength of the first. Which control a certification authority should honor is stated nowhere, so a request carrying more than one is now refused with `crmf/bad-controls`, as `pki.possession.verifyRequest` already refused the equivalent PKCS#10 attribute. A repeated CMS signed attribute was already refused by the shared parser; a CRMF control is a different structure and was not.

`pki.possession.verifyRequest` and `pki.possession.statementOf` read only the first `statementOfPossession` attribute of a request that carries several, so every binding check on the rest was skipped. A request carrying a sound statement followed by one naming a different certificate was accepted on the strength of the first. A request carrying more than one is now refused with `possession/bad-request` at both doors, which is what `pki.schema.csr` and `pki.cms` already did for the attribute sets they read.

`pki.possession.verifyRequest` read only the first `extensionRequest` attribute of a request that carries several, and every check RFC 9883 asks for reads the extensions a request asks for. A request naming `keyAgreement` in its first attribute and `digitalSignature` in its second was therefore reported as not requesting a signature certificate, which is the section 6 prohibition, and a later subjectAltName request could escape the section 3 comparison the same way. Which attribute a CA should honor is stated nowhere, so a request carrying more than one is now refused with `possession/bad-request`, as `pki.schema.csr.decodeExtensions` already refused it.

`pki.possession.verifyRequest` did not treat a DSA subject key as signature-only, so a request to certify one, which can only ever sign, did not engage the RFC 9883 prohibition the way an EdDSA, RSASSA-PSS, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA key does. DSA is now in that set.

The receipt `pki.ct.addChain` and `pki.ct.addPreChain` return omitted `logIdHex`, the field the log-list verbs key a log by, so a receipt those verbs had just verified could not be handed to them: `pki.ct.verifySctWithLogList` refused it with `ct/bad-input` and `pki.ct.verifySctList` dropped it and reported a policy failure. The field is present now, matching what `pki.ct.parseSctList` and `pki.ct.signSct` produce, so a receipt round-trips through every verb in the module that reads one.

`pki.tsp.verify` reported `tsp/unsupported-algorithm` for a timestamp token bound to its certificate by an `ESSCertID` v1. That structure carries no hash algorithm field because the type fixes it at SHA-1, so nothing was unsupported: the algorithm is known and the binding is collision-weak, which the refusal already intended and the code contradicted. It reports `tsp/weak-digest` now, as does an `ESSCertIDv2` naming SHA-1 explicitly. The refusal itself is unchanged, and an `ESSCertIDv2` naming an algorithm this build cannot compute keeps `tsp/unsupported-algorithm`. An absent field carries the type's default; an unrecognized field names an algorithm nothing can compute.

`pki.cms.sign` refused to emit two instances of one unsigned attribute type, citing RFC 5652 sec. 5.3. That clause states no such rule: `UnsignedAttributes` is a `SET SIZE (1..MAX) OF Attribute`, the clause says of the field only that it "is a collection of attributes that are not signed", and the uniqueness rules the RFC does state are per type, one instance of the message-digest attribute among the signed ones, while sec. 11.4's countersignature type "specifies one or more signatures". The refusal denied a conforming message, and the shape it denied is the ordinary one: a signature re-timestamped by several authorities carries one timestamp-token attribute per authority. Repeated unsigned attribute types are emitted now, and the per-type rules with a clause behind them are kept, so a content-type, message-digest or signing-time attribute is still refused among the unsigned ones. The signed side still emits at most one instance of each type, which is stricter than the RFC asks and is now described that way rather than attributed to sec. 5.3.

`pki.tuf.verifySignatures` refused an RSA signature whose PSS salt is longer than the digest. The `rsassa-pss-sha256` scheme states the hash and the padding and says nothing about the salt length, which is the signer's to choose, and the reference implementation signs with the longest salt the modulus allows, so metadata that verifies elsewhere was reported unverified here and the root rotation it carried could not be applied. The salt length is now read from the signature, where it is carried, while the hash and the padding stay fixed by the scheme name: a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature under the same key is still refused. Every other RSASSA-PSS verifier in the toolkit keeps its pinned salt length, because the format declares one and the declaration is authenticated: `pki.cms.verify` reads it from the RSASSA-PSS AlgorithmIdentifier, `pki.path.validate` from the certificate, and `pki.jose.verify` from the RFC 7518 row for PS256, PS384 and PS512.

The Certificate Transparency verbs copied a caller's bytes and then refused them against a size cap, so an input over the cap was allocated before it was rejected. Measured, a 64 MiB SCT-list extension value, log-list JSON, certificate, or SCT extensions or signature field each allocated its full size before drawing the refusal. The one door these verbs take their bytes through now measures the cap on a view that shares the caller's store, before the copy, so `pki.ct.parseSctList`, `pki.ct.verifyLogListSignature`, `pki.ct.reconstructSignedData` and `pki.ct.encodeSctList` refuse an oversized input without allocating it, and a log-list JSON passed as a string is sized with `Buffer.byteLength` rather than encoded first. Each refusal keeps the code it had, except that an over-cap SCT-list value now reports `ct/too-large` rather than whatever the discarded copy failed to decode as.

`pki.altSig.verify` and the other `pki.altSig` verbs checked which format their input was without checking that it is a well-formed one of that format, then read extensions out of it directly. A certificate carrying the `altSignatureValue` extension twice was therefore verified successfully: the verb read the first of the two and the preimage it reconstructed removed both, while `pki.schema.x509.parse` refuses the same bytes with `x509/duplicate-extension`. The structure is parsed before any extension is read, so every rule the shared parser enforces holds here too.

`pki.crmf.build` did not recognize a `statementOfPossession` supplied through the pre-encoded `controls` array, only through the object form, so it resolved the proof-of-possession algorithm from the key being certified rather than from the signature certificate the statement names. Building an X25519 request with a pre-encoded statement therefore failed with `crmf/unsupported-algorithm` while the identical request in object form succeeded. Both forms now resolve the signing certificate the same way, and a pre-encoded statement that does not decode, or that omits its certificate, is refused with `crmf/bad-controls` rather than passed over.

Byte-taking verbs across the toolkit accepted a Buffer and a `Uint8Array` but refused a `DataView` or an `ArrayBuffer` carrying the same bytes, although each advertises the whole set and one names it outright: "ikm must be a byte source (Buffer / TypedArray / DataView / ArrayBuffer)". An `ArrayBuffer` is what `Response.arrayBuffer()` and `crypto.subtle.exportKey("raw", ...)` return, so the refused half is the half a caller is most often holding, and the refusal blamed the content for the container. In `pki.tlog` it was worse than a refusal: `parseTile`, `parseNote`, `parseEntryBundle`, `parseCheckpoint` and `keyId` threw a bare `TypeError` with no code for an `ArrayBuffer`, so a caller could not branch on it and a fuzz harness could not tell it from a crash. Fixed at `pki.tlog` (all five verbs), `pki.hpke` (`info`, `aad`, plaintext, `ikm` and the exporter context), `pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` (the pinned `rekorKeys` and `ctLogs` material), `pki.tuf.verifySignatures` (`metadata.signedBytes`), `pki.ct` (the pinned log key on `getSth`, `getProofByHash` and `fetchLogList`, the SCT fields, and an issuer named by its SubjectPublicKeyInfo) and every format's `decodeExtension`. The size cap still runs before any copy, because normalizing shares the caller's buffer rather than duplicating it. Shared memory stays refused, and a key is still a `KeyObject`, a Buffer or the `{ pkm }` wrapper, which the refusal now names exactly instead of saying "a raw buffer".

`pki.path.crlChecker` and `pki.path.ocspChecker` take a list. Handed a single CRL or response, which is the natural slip, they mapped over whatever arrived: a `DataView`, an `ArrayBuffer` or a plain object produced a bare `TypeError` naming an internal expression, and a single CRL Buffer was mapped over its bytes and reported the first byte as a malformed CRL. Both now refuse a non-list with `path/bad-input` naming the argument. An omitted or empty list still means there is nothing to check.

`pki.tlog.verifyNote` and `pki.tlog.verifyCheckpoint` chose the digest for an ECDSA signature from the key's curve, so a conforming note signed by a P-384 or P-521 log key was refused with `tlog/bad-signature` and only P-256 logs interoperated. Signature type `0x02` is defined by c2sp.org/signed-note as "ECDSA signatures as implemented by github.com/transparency-dev/witness", whose verifier computes a SHA-256 digest for every key it accepts; the digest belongs to the signature type, not to the key. All three curves the specification admits are now verified under SHA-256, and a signature made with the digest the curve would suggest is refused. The curve allowlist is unchanged: a key on any other curve is still `tlog/bad-input`.

`pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` refused a bundle whose certificate chain carries more than one intermediate with the same subject where only one of them is the real issuer, which is the shape a CA key rotation produces. Three things had to change, and together they make the verdict independent of the order the bundle lists its certificates in. The search now backtracks instead of taking the first intermediate matching an issuer name, as `pki.path.build` already did. It offers every path it finds rather than one, so an intermediate that matches by name and then fails validation no longer hides the sibling that would have validated. And it tries a candidate that completes the path before one that does not, so a chain padded with same-subject intermediates cannot consume the search. The work is bounded: at most 8 paths, 256 search steps and a depth of 16, so a chain carrying many same-subject intermediates is abandoned rather than explored.

`pki.transport.peerChain` and `pki fetch` described their chain as the certificates the endpoint presented. It is the chain the TLS session resolved, which is not the same thing: the runtime completes the chain from the trust anchors in scope, so an endpoint that sends only its leaf still yields the entries above it and those came from a configured anchor rather than from the wire. Node exposes no API for the transmitted list, so the distinction is stated rather than guessed at, and filtering entries that match an anchor would drop a root an endpoint really did send. The verb's documentation, the `pki fetch` usage text and the line it writes to stderr now say which chain this is, and point at `peerCertificate` for the one certificate the endpoint certainly sent. No behavior changed.

The RFC 9883 citations named the wrong sections. The prohibition "The privateKeyPossessionStatement attribute MUST NOT be used to obtain a signature certificate" is in section 6, not section 4, and the two name comparisons whose resolution the RFC leaves to the certificate policy are in section 3, not section 4. The refusal messages `pki.possession.verifyRequest` reports, the `citation` field of `lint/rfc9883/signature-certificate-requested`, and the CRMF proof-of-possession note, which belongs to section 5, now each name the clause they enforce.

The check that every internal fail-closed guard declares how its shape is kept from being re-inlined read a module's exported names with a pattern that recognized `module.exports = {` and `module.exports = Object.freeze({`. The guard modules export through a freeze reached by another name, so the check read 18 of the 19 as exporting nothing and passed over every function in them: 13 guards had no declaration and nothing said so. The pattern now matches the wrapper as any callee, and the 13 declarations are in place. No shipped behavior changes; the gate that was meant to prevent a guard shipping without enforcement now does.
